books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek Treaty), September 17, 1851

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek Treaty), September 17, 1851, Articles 1, 2, 3, and 7, as signed. Public domain. Note: the Senate ratified the treaty with an amendment changing the Article 7 annuity from fifty years to ten years (plus up to five discretionary years), May 24, 1852.
stimulus.text: The aforesaid nations... do hereby covenant and agree to abstain in future from all hostilities whatever against each other... The aforesaid nations do hereby recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts, within their respective territories... In consideration of the rights and privileges acknowledged in the preceding article, the United States bind themselves to protect the aforesaid Indian nations against the commission of all depredations by the people of the said United States... the United States bind themselves to deliver to the said Indian nations the sum of Fifty thousand dollars per annum for fifty years in provisions, merchandize, domestic animals and agricultural implement.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Treaty of Fort Laramie, September 17, 1851, public domain
stem: The treaty's promise of $50,000 a year in goods for fifty years best illustrates which of the following?

options.text: The United States' plan to buy all tribal land at once.
options.misconception: The payments were annuities for peace and passage, not a purchase price for all tribal land.

options.text: Yearly payments to secure peace and safe passage for migrants.
The tribes' demand for cash payment in gold coin.
options.misconception: The payments were in provisions, merchandise, animals, and implements — goods, not gold coin.

options.text: The federal government's decision to end all trade with the tribes.
options.misconception: The treaty set up regular yearly deliveries of goods, which is trade continued, not ended.

rationales.A: The annuity was payment for peace and for roads and posts, not a purchase of all tribal land at once.
rationales.B: The treaty traded peace and the right to build roads and posts for fifty years of yearly goods — payments that bought safe passage for the migrants streaming west. Background: about 10,000 Plains Indians had gathered near Fort Laramie for the council.
rationales.C: The payments were goods — provisions, merchandise, animals, and implements — not gold coin.
rationales.D: Yearly deliveries of goods are trade continued on a schedule, not trade ended.
rationales.general:
1. Find what the money bought. The tribes promised peace and allowed roads and military posts; the United States promised fifty years of goods.
2. Ask why the government paid. Wagon trains were crossing tribal land, and the government wanted the crossing safe.
3. Read the goods list. Provisions, merchandise, animals, and implements — supplies for living, not a land price.
Remember: an annuity is a bargain stretched over time. The United States was renting peace and passage, year by year.
